newsitem.title: POLAND: Zloty to test resistance next wk, bond yields rise.
newsitem.headline: Zloty to test resistance next wk, bond yields rise.

text.p: The recently tarnished Polish zloty may regain its shine next week and push upward to key resistance at 2.5 percent from parity, despite the likelihood of another wave of central bank interventions.

Analysts said the zloty may have enough strength to break this obstacle when foreigners pay for fixed bonds bought earlier in January. It spent this week drifting mainly sideways, in the absence of moves from the central bank.
"Payments for bonds may strengthen the zloty next week and pit it right against the big barrier at 2.5 percent," said Karol Zaluski, forex dealer at ING bank in Warsaw.

Analysts said foreign investors may already have zlotys for much of the $50 million of bonds they bought at the January 16 tender, but that the market would still likely regain its pro-zloty mentality and test the central bank's resistance.
Last week repeated National Bank of Poland interventions blasted the zloty nearly two percentage points lower from highs touching four percent from above its trading band centre.
At 1200 GMT on Friday, the zloty was at 2.37/2.31 percent from parity, against last week's close at 2.31/2.25 percent.
It was at 3.0005/20 to the dollar and at 1.8368/75 to the mark, against last week's 2.9895/15 and 1.8330/40.
Analysts said exchange rate fluctuations over the last several weeks would likely keep many foreign investors at bay at Monday's primary T-bill auction despite expectations of slightly higher yields.

"The NBP scared away many more speculative-minded investors which play on exchange rate fluctuations," said Wojciech Kowalczyk, senior dealer at Bank Handlowy SA. "However, foreign interest in Polish bonds remains high," he added.

Analysts said the benchmark 52-week T-bill yield may pierce 20 percent after a 19.97 average yield at last Monday's tender, while 13- and 26-week bill yields should inch up to 19.70 and 19.85 percent from 19.55 and 19.80 percent respectively.
Dealers said demand should fall shy of the treasury's one billion zloty offer as banks continued to be drawn by the more attractive NBP-bills with yields at 22.00 percent.
"The Treasury's larger offer should translate into higher yields especially because banks can get their hands on NBP-bills," said Bartlomiej Kumela dealer at Societe Generale.

Analysts said this week's central bank decision to raise obligatory reserves on call deposits on February 28 would have no effect on the market in ther near-term as rates were more closely connected to the scope of NBP drainage operations.

"Nothing indicates that yields on NBP-bills will decline and the NBP's move (to increase required reserves) was aimed at cooling credit action and limiting money supply growth," Societe's Kumela said.
